newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 13.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 13.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Amendments to the New South Wales Industrial Relations Act introduced last year by the state's Labor bovernment now mean that senior executives who have been unfairly treated can gain payouts of thousands, and potentially millions, of dollars. The change are a far cry from the days when executives on high salaries suffered a lack of employment security. Page 1.

The Australian Industrial Relations Commission will be obliged to take a more adversarial stance when hearing unfair dismissal cases under new legislation introduced by the federal government, said Steven Amendola, a partner in the law firm Dunhill Maden Butler. Page 4.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission commissioner for native title, Geoff Clark, has urged state governments to negotiate with Aboriginal groups following the Wik decision. This would avoid legal battles and large compensation payouts he said while speaking at the launch of the "plain English" guide to the Wik judgement, put out by ATSIC. Page 5.

Finance Minister John Fahey said yesterday that the government was on track to achieve its targeted A$1 billion surplus within the current parliamentary term. He said this would be done without any new major spending cuts and he called on the Senate to pass the remaining savings measures from last year's budget worth about A$1 billion over four years. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

After receiving legal advice, state and federal government officials believe up to 70 percent of Australia could be open to native title claims following the High Court's Wik decision. The claim increased pressure on Prime Minister John Howard to respon forcefully to the Wik judgement. Page 1.

Rescued English yachtsman Tony Bullimore yesterday thanked God for his life during a moving prayer service on board HMAS Adelaide. Bullimore was joined by fellow survivor Thierry Dubois of France, who, along with Bullimore, was saved last week from the Southern Ocean by Australia's navy and air force. Page 1.

Australian tennis player Mark Philippoussis has withdrawn from the Australian Tennis Open after suffering from tendonitis in his right elbow. His withdrawal is bad news for the organisers of the event, who will lose their local drawcard, but even worse for Philippoussis, who, at 20, is expected to suffer the injury on and off during his career. Page 1.

Acting Treasurer John Fahey said yesterday the federal government may have to cut spending in the May Budget by up to A$1.75 billion because of Senate obstructionism. Fahey clearly stated that ministers wishing to include new spending incentives in the next budget would need to provide offsetting savings to protect its bottom line. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Federal Finance Minister John Fahey said yesterday that tax incentives for saving, that may be funded from the A$4 billion set aside for the former government's tax cuts, are high on the federal government's agenda for the May Budget. Fahey added that a new round of spending cuts in the budget may be introduced to make it easier for the government to introduce changes, such as its own national savings scheme. Page 1.

Australia's Civil Aviation Safety Authority has confirmed international air safety authorities are expected to order expensive modifications to Boeing 747s if it is found that the TWA crash off New York in July was the result of an explosion in a fuel tank. Australia's fleet would be ordered to be modified if the crash investigators recommend changes to later model 747s. Page 1.

Australia will miss the one day international cricket finals for the first time since the 1979/80 series after the West Indies' miraculous defeat over Australia at the WACA Ground in Perth yesterday. West Indian batsman Brian Lara hit a match-winning 90 to pull his team up to win. Page 1.

The New South Wales Department of Gaming is undertaking sweeping changes to the state's TAB that will see about 120 unprofitable TAB agencies closed over the next three years and punters possibly able to place their bets at service stations, newsagencies and pharmacies in rural and outer-suburban areas. Page 1.
THE AGE

Documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act show the tendering process for a multi-million dollar Victorian Government contract to test Victorian livestock for disease was marred by allegations of ethical breaches and unfair treatment. The documents show that the committee assessing the bidding, which was finally won by Victorian Veterinary Pathology Services, was divided over the outcome. Page A1.

Police believe Geelong West grandmother, Edna Joyce Findlay, 75, was severely injured moments before her house was deliberately set alight around 3 am yesterday morning. The damage to the house makes it difficult for police to determine if anything was stolen, but there is suspicion the woman's death was the result of a robbery gone wrong. Page A3.

The journal Australian Social Work claims that child protection services in Victoria are less effective than they were in 1993 due to the introduction of mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse combined with reduced funding. This had resulted in a huge increase in the investigative workload for the child protection system, with much of the family support role now being off-loaded to non-government welfare agencies. Page A1.

Fees at Victorian private schools have risen six percent, three times the rate of inflation, in the past year. The rise has been blamed by the Association of Independent Schools of Victoria on a 12 percent pay rise for teachers, recently negotiated beteen unions and employers. Increases in infrastructure and equipment costs were also responsible for the rises, those in the industry claimed. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
